**The Imjin War (1592–1598)** | Aspect | Details | |--------|---------| | **Name** | Imjin War (임진왜란) – “Imjin” refers to the Chinese year 1592 (甲辰) in the sexagenary cycle. | | **Belligerents** | • **Japan** – led by Toyotomi Hideyoshi, seeking to conquer Korea and expand influence into China.
• **Joseon Korea** – the Korean kingdom, allied with Ming China.
• **Ming China** – sent troops to aid Joseon after Korea’s request. | | **Timeline** | • **April 1592** – Japanese forces land at Busan and begin a rapid advance.
• **Late 1592** – Korean forces, with Ming support, push back and recapture Seoul.

• **1597–1598** – Japanese forces retreat; final battles end with the death of Hideyoshi and the withdrawal of Japanese troops. | | **Key Battles** | • **Battle of Hansan Island** (May 1592) – Korean naval victory under Admiral Yi Sun-sin.
• **Battle of Myeongnyang** (October 1597) – Yi Sun-sin defeats a larger Japanese fleet with only 13 ships.
• **Battle of Noryang** (December 1598) – final naval engagement; Japanese forces surrender. | | **Causes** | • Hideyoshi’s ambition to conquer China via Korea.
• Korea’s strategic position as a gateway to the Chinese mainland.
• Japan’s desire to secure trade routes and political influence. | | **Consequences** | • Massive destruction in Korea: cities, temples, and infrastructure were devastated.
• Loss of life: estimates range from 200,000–400,000 Korean civilians and soldiers, and 30,000–50,000 Japanese troops.
• Strengthened Korean naval tactics and the legacy of Admiral Yi Sun-sin.
• Set the stage for future Sino‑Japanese conflicts and influenced Korean national identity. | | **Cultural Impact** | • The war is commemorated in Korean history as a period of resilience and patriotism.
• Yi Sun-sin’s “turtle ships” and naval strategies are celebrated in literature, film, and monuments.
• The war’s legacy informs modern Korean views on defense and foreign policy. | **Quick Takeaway:** The Imjin War was a major conflict where Japan attempted to invade Korea, but Korean forces—supported by Ming China—managed to repel the invasion, preserving Korean sovereignty and leaving a lasting legacy in East Asian history.
